html:
A Sufi brotherhood founded in Konya by the followers of the poet Rumi after his death in 1273. In the West its members are known as the whirling dervishes.

Rumi's son Sultan Walad shaped the circle around his father into an order with rules, lodges and a line of leaders from Rumi's family. Its signature rite is the sema: dervishes in white robes and tall felt hats turn slowly to music of reed flute and drum, a form of dhikr, the remembrance of God. The order taught a gentle, learned form of Sufism built around Rumi's Masnavi.

Konya was then a city of the Sultanate of Rum. Under the Ottoman Empire the order spread to lodges from the Balkans to Cairo and found favour at court; several sultans were patrons, and its music shaped Ottoman classical music.

In 1925 the young Turkish Republic under Atatürk closed all Sufi lodges. Rumi's tomb in Konya became a museum. The sema survives as a performance and a living rite, and the order carries on abroad and quietly in Turkey.
